pisco: Pisco grew out of the vineyards Spanish settlers planted in Peru's southern coastal valleys in the 16th century, and a 1613 will from Ica, often cited as the earliest record of the spirit, lists a copper still and jars of grape aguardiente. The name comes from the port of Pisco, through which it was shipped, and is on record for the drink by 1764. Chile developed its own tradition in the Elqui and Limarí valleys and set out its rules in 1931, Peru defined its denomination of origin in 1991, and the two countries still dispute who owns the name.
poire-williams: The pear came first: the Williams' Bon Chrétien was raised in Berkshire, England, in the 18th century and spread under the name of Richard Williams, the nurseryman who sold it. Its strong perfume carries through the still, and pear eau-de-vie became a speciality of Alsace, Switzerland's Valais and the Black Forest, with the Morand distillery in Martigny registering the name Williamine for its own. The pear-in-the-bottle versions are made by slipping glass over young fruit on the tree in spring and leaving it to ripen inside.
slivovitz: Plum brandy has been distilled from the Balkans to Bohemia for centuries, and its name comes from the Slavic word for plum, sliva. It grew up as a farm and village spirit, made from orchard fruit at small stills and kept for family occasions, which is why Serbia, Bosnia, Croatia, the Czech lands, Slovakia, Poland and Hungary each have their own version and spelling. The EU settled competing claims by treating slivovitz as a generic name that countries can qualify with their own, and UNESCO has inscribed the Serbian customs around šljivovica on its intangible heritage list.
batavia-arrack: Batavia arrack is named after Batavia, the port the Dutch East India Company founded on Java in 1619 on the site of today's Jakarta. Chinese distillers in and around the town made it from sugarcane molasses fermented with red rice, and the Company shipped it to Europe, where it became a mainstay of the punch bowl. Sweden took to it after its own East India ships began returning from Asia in the 1730s, and arrack became the base of Swedish punsch, which is still made with it today.
cachaca: Cachaça is usually traced to the sugar mills that followed the arrival of cane cuttings in Brazil from Madeira in 1532, where fermented cane juice was soon being distilled. The spirit was built on the labour of enslaved people on those plantations, and it grew popular enough that Portugal tried to ban it in 1635 to protect its own grape brandy. A revolt in Rio de Janeiro helped win legalisation on 13 September 1661, the date Brazil now marks as National Cachaça Day. In 2013 the United States agreed to recognise cachaça as a distinctively Brazilian product.
pitorro: Pitorro is Puerto Rico's home-distilled cane spirit, made for generations in small backyard and hillside stills outside the licensing system, which is why it is often called the island's moonshine rum. Its makers have left few written records, and it goes by other names too, such as cañita, after the thin copper tubing of the still. Curing it traditionally means burying the jugs in the ground for a time, and much of it is steeped with fruit and spices and turned into coquito at Christmas, when the authorities also step up their pursuit of unlicensed producers.
barrel-aged-gin: Gin has met wood before: in the 18th and 19th centuries gin and genever were commonly shipped and stored in casks, and some picked up colour on the way. The modern category is a revival rather than an unbroken line, taking shape this century as craft distillers in the United States and Europe began resting gin in oak on purpose. Rules differ from market to market, so labels such as aged, reserve or barrel rested can mean quite different things from one producer to the next.
contemporary-gin: Contemporary gin has no single founding moment, but Hendrick's, launched by William Grant & Sons from its Girvan distillery in Scotland in 1999 with cucumber and rose among its botanicals, is often taken as the turning point. In 2006 bartender Ryan Magarian and distiller Christian Krogstad released Aviation Gin in Portland, Oregon, and Magarian's label for the style, New Western Dry, gave the idea a name. The craft distilling boom that followed spread it worldwide, with makers building gins around local plants rather than a classic juniper-first recipe.
genever: Genever began as a medicine in the Low Countries, where juniper berries were distilled with wine, and the Antwerp physician Philippus Hermanni printed one of the first recipes in the 16th century. By 1606 the Dutch were taxing it as a drink, and as cold winters ruined Flemish vineyards, distillers switched to malt wine made from grain. The popular claim that Leiden professor Franciscus Sylvius invented it does not hold up, since he was born after those taxes. English soldiers fighting in the Low Countries brought home a taste for it, the story said to lie behind the phrase Dutch courage.
london-dry-gin: London dry took shape in the 19th century, after the continuous column still, developed by Robert Stein and refined by Aeneas Coffey, gave distillers a clean, strong spirit that no longer needed sugar to hide rough flavours. London's distillers used it to make unsweetened, juniper-led gins, and the city's name stuck to the method rather than the place. Today the term is a legal category: all the botanicals must go in during redistillation in a traditional still, with only water and a trace of sugar allowed afterwards, so a London dry gin can be made anywhere.
navy-strength-gin: Navy strength means gin at about 57% ABV, or 100 degrees on the old British proof scale, the strength at which spirit-soaked gunpowder will still burn. The usual story ties it to the Royal Navy, whose gin was stored near the powder and had to be strong enough that a leak would not ruin it. Historians treat that story with some caution, since proving spirit with gunpowder was a general test rather than a naval one, and the label owes much of its modern popularity to Plymouth Gin, whose navy strength bottling traditionally went into the commissioning kits presented to new Royal Navy ships.
old-tom-gin: Old Tom was the sweetened gin of 18th- and 19th-century England, made when spirits were rough and sugar helped smooth them. The usual story of the name goes back to the gin restrictions of 1736, when Captain Dudley Bradstreet wrote that he sold gin through a pipe under the sign of a cat at a London window, and cat signs were later said to mark gin sold the same way. It appears in early recipes for the Tom Collins and the Martinez, faded as London dry took over in the early 20th century, and returned when Hayman's relaunched one based on an old family recipe, followed by many other distillers.
sloe-gin: Sloe gin is an English country tradition with no recorded inventor, born of the habit of steeping the tart fruit of the blackthorn, a common hedgerow shrub, in gin with sugar to make something drinkable from berries too sour to eat raw. It was long made at home each autumn, and commercial versions from gin distillers kept the style on shop shelves. Custom says to pick the sloes after the first frost to soften their skins, though many makers now freeze them instead, and EU rules require at least 25% ABV for a liqueur to be sold as sloe gin.
benedictine: Bénédictine was launched in 1863 by Alexandre Le Grand, a wine merchant in Fécamp, Normandy, who developed it with a local chemist and said he had rebuilt it from a lost recipe of the town's Benedictine abbey, which the brand dates to 1510; historians see that monastic link as marketing. He built the Palais Bénédictine to make and promote it, and a drier blend with brandy, B&B, followed in the 1930s. Soldiers of the East Lancashire Regiment are said to have brought the taste home from France after the First World War, and the Burnley Miners' Club is reputedly its largest single customer.
drambuie: Drambuie as a brand begins on the Isle of Skye, where James Ross, owner of the Broadford Hotel, made the liqueur and registered its name as a trademark in 1893. The name is usually explained as Gaelic for the drink that satisfies. The romantic part of the story, that Bonnie Prince Charlie gave the recipe to the MacKinnon clan as thanks for sheltering him after the failed Jacobite rising, is family legend that historians dispute. After Ross's death his widow sold the recipe to Malcolm MacKinnon, who began producing it commercially in Edinburgh around 1910.
genepi: Génépi is a mountain household liqueur of the French and Italian Alps, made in Savoie, the Aosta Valley and Piedmont by steeping or distilling small alpine wormwoods of the Artemisia family. Its exact beginnings are not recorded; it grew from the old Alpine habit of preserving wild herbs in spirit, and the drink simply took the local name of the plants themselves. Because the wild plants are scarce, picking them is restricted in parts of the Alps, much génépi today is made from cultivated plants, and several alpine génépis now carry protected geographical indications.
green-chartreuse: Green Chartreuse traces back to 1605, when François Annibal d'Estrées gave the Carthusian monks of Vauvert, in Paris, an alchemical manuscript for an elixir of long life. The recipe reached the order's mother house, the Grande Chartreuse in the mountains near Grenoble, where apothecary brother Jérôme Maubec is credited with working out a usable formula in 1737, and the green liqueur for drinking was later developed from it. Its colour gave the shade chartreuse its name, the order says only two monks at a time know the full recipe of some 130 plants, and the monks now cap how much they make.
yellow-chartreuse: The Carthusian monks date Yellow Chartreuse to 1838, when the community of the Grande Chartreuse, in the mountains near Grenoble, created a milder, sweeter and lower-strength companion to their green liqueur from the same family of plants. Like the green, it takes its name from the monastery and its Chartreuse mountains. Its production followed the monks into exile in Tarragona, Spain, after French law expelled the order in 1903, before returning to France, and the recipe remains with the order, which still decides how much is made.
irish-blended-whiskey: Blends existed in Ireland before, but the style became the country's mainstream after 1966, when the surviving Dublin and Cork distillers merged as Irish Distillers to save an industry that had collapsed since its 19th-century heyday. In 1975 they moved production to a new distillery at Midleton, County Cork, able to make pot still, malt and column-distilled grain spirit under one roof, and brands such as Jameson and Powers were rebuilt as blends of the three. By the mid-1970s only Midleton and Bushmills were working on the island, and the blended style carried Irish whiskey's revival.
irish-single-malt: Ireland's malt whiskey heritage is usually dated to 1608, when King James I granted Sir Thomas Phillips a licence to distil in County Antrim, the date Old Bushmills prints on its bottles, although the distillery company itself was formally established much later. For most of Irish history malt played second fiddle to pot still and later blended whiskey, and Bushmills kept the single malt style alive almost alone. The independent Cooley distillery, founded by John Teeling in 1987, broke the industry's monopoly and added more single malts, and Ireland's 2014 technical file formally defined the category.
irish-single-pot-still: Single pot still whiskey is usually traced to a 1785 tax on malted barley, which pushed Irish distillers to add raw, unmalted barley to their mash and run it through large copper pot stills. The spicy, creamy style that resulted outlived the tax and became the signature of Dublin's great 19th-century distilleries, when Irish whiskey was the most popular in the world. After the industry's collapse it survived mainly at Midleton, in bottlings such as Redbreast and Green Spot, and Ireland's 2014 technical file gave single pot still its legal definition.
poitin: Poitín takes its name from the Irish pota, the small pot still its makers used, and it became an outlaw's spirit when 17th-century excise laws, usually dated to 1661, made unlicensed distilling illegal. For more than three centuries it was made in hidden stills from grain, potatoes, whey or molasses, and the poitín maker dodging the excise man became a figure of Irish folklore. Licensed poitín was later allowed for export, and in 1997 for sale at home, and since 2008 Irish poitín has held EU geographical indication status.
advocaat: Commercial advocaat is often credited to J.G. Cooymans, who opened a distillery in 's-Hertogenbosch in 1828 and developed the egg drink there. Two explanations compete for the name: one says Dutch colonists in Brazil met an avocado drink and recreated its texture with egg yolks back home, while an 1882 Dutch dictionary calls it advocatenborrel, a lawyer's drink, smooth enough to ease the throat of someone who must speak in public. In Britain it found a second life in the Snowball, mixed with lemonade.
allspice-dram: Allspice dram is a Jamaican liqueur, known on the island as pimento dram, made by steeping the dried berries of the pimento tree in rum and sweetening it. Its exact beginnings are not recorded, but it belongs to Jamaica's long role as the main source of allspice, a spice the English named for the way it seems to combine cinnamon, nutmeg and clove. Tiki bartenders used it in the mid-20th century, and after it all but disappeared from American shelves, importer Haus Alpenz brought it back as St. Elizabeth Allspice Dram, which returned it to cocktail menus.
amaretto: Saronno's favourite legend dates amaretto to the early sixteenth century, when the painter Bernardino Luini, a follower of Leonardo, was working on frescoes in the town's sanctuary and a widowed innkeeper who modelled for his Madonna is said to have given him a liqueur of apricot kernels steeped in brandy. The tale is unproven, but it gave the town its claim. The name is a diminutive of amaro, bitter, after the bitter almond or kernel flavour, and the Reina family's Amaretto di Saronno, now sold as Disaronno, carried the style around the world.
blue-curacao: Blue curaçao is the colourful offshoot of orange curaçao, the liqueur flavoured with the peel of the bitter laraha orange of Curaçao. Bols was selling a blue version by 1912, under the name Crème de Ciel, cream of the sky, with the colour added purely for show, since it tastes much like the orange original. It found its lasting role in the tiki era, notably in the Blue Hawaii that bartender Harry Yee is credited with creating in Waikiki in 1957, and has tinted tropical drinks ever since.
coffee-liqueur: Coffee liqueurs have older roots, but the style's best-known brand began in 1936 in Veracruz, Mexico, when Kahlúa was first produced there from arabica coffee, sugarcane spirit and vanilla. Jamaica's Tia Maria followed after the Second World War, and the two became fixtures of post-war bars around the world. Coffee liqueur found its two most famous homes in the White Russian, with vodka and cream, and in the Espresso Martini, which London bartender Dick Bradsell is credited with creating in the 1980s.
creme-de-cassis: Blackcurrants were steeped in spirit as a ratafia in Burgundy long before, but modern crème de cassis is dated to 1841, when Dijon café owner Auguste-Denis Lagoute made a richer, sweeter liqueur from the region's berries. It caught on in the city's cafés, and Burgundy remains its heartland, with Crème de Cassis de Bourgogne protected as a geographical indication since 2015. Its partner drink, white wine with cassis, took the name kir from Canon Félix Kir, the Resistance figure and long-serving mayor of Dijon who poured it for visiting dignitaries.
creme-de-menthe: Mint liqueurs are old, but one of the oldest names still sold, Get, dates to 1796, when the brothers Jean and Pierre Get began making peppermint liqueur in Revel, near Toulouse; it survives today as Get 27 and Get 31. The crème in the name refers to its high sugar and syrupy texture rather than any dairy. In the United States it became a staple of the Stinger, with brandy, and of the Grasshopper, which Tujague's restaurant in New Orleans says its owner Philibert Guichet created in the early 20th century.
creme-de-violette: Violet liqueurs belong to the 19th-century European fashion for flower cordials, with Toulouse, a city famous for its violets, and Austria among their homes. In America crème de violette is remembered mainly for the Aviation, the gin, lemon and maraschino cocktail recorded by New York bartender Hugo Ensslin, whose violet note gave the drink its pale sky colour. The liqueur all but vanished from US shelves for decades until importer Haus Alpenz brought in the Austrian Rothman & Winter, which made the original Aviation possible to mix again.
elderflower-liqueur: Elderflower cordials have long been a European country tradition, but elderflower liqueur as a bar staple dates to 2007, when Robert Cooper, from a family of liqueur makers, launched St-Germain, made with elderflowers gathered in the French Alps of Savoie. Cooper had been struck by an elderflower cocktail in a London bar, and his liqueur spread so quickly through cocktail menus that bartenders nicknamed it bartender's ketchup. Bacardi bought the brand in 2013, and many other producers have since made their own.
falernum: Falernum is a Barbadian creation, thought to have begun in the 18th century as a homemade spiced mixture of lime and rum, and John D. Taylor's of Bridgetown dates its Velvet Falernum recipe to 1890. An 1892 magazine described it as a curious liqueur of rum and lime juice, and it appeared in American bar manuals by the 1930s. The name is debated: some link it to Falernian, the prized wine of ancient Rome, while a Bajan folk explanation says it comes from you have fuh learn um, the instruction for getting the mix right. Versions without alcohol are made as a syrup.
irish-cream: Irish cream was invented as a brand: Baileys was developed in London in 1971 by a team working for Gilbeys of Ireland, among them David Gluckman, Hugh Seymour-Davies and Tom Jago, and it was launched in 1974. Their first mix of Irish whiskey and cream tasted harsh until they stirred in powdered drinking chocolate, and the name was borrowed from Bailey's Bistro, a small restaurant below their office on Greek Street in Soho. Once they had solved how to keep cream and spirit stable on the shelf, dozens of other Irish cream brands followed.
limoncello: Limoncello's birthplace is claimed by several places around the Bay of Naples, with Sorrento, the Amalfi coast and Capri each telling its own version. The story most often cited comes from Capri, where the grandmother of Maria Antonia Farace is said to have made it in the early 20th century, while others argue that monks or fishermen made it much earlier, and one account even places it in Sicily. Whoever was first, it rests on the region's thick-skinned, fragrant lemons, now protected as the Limone di Sorrento and Limone Costa d'Amalfi IGPs.
maraschino-liqueur: Maraschino comes from Zadar on the Dalmatian coast, then the Venetian-ruled city of Zara, where liqueurs were made from the local sour marasca cherry. Industrial production began in 1759, when Venetian merchant Francesco Drioli opened a distillery there, and Girolamo Luxardo founded his in 1821, the name that still leads the category. After the Second World War, Zadar became part of Yugoslavia and the Luxardo family rebuilt in Torreglia, near Padua, replanting marasca orchards from scratch, while the Zadar factories were merged into Maraska, which still makes maraschino in the city.
nocino: Nocino is a farmhouse liqueur of Emilia-Romagna, above all the province of Modena, made by steeping green, unripe walnuts in spirit with sugar and spices. Its age is uncertain: Italian monasteries are said to have made walnut liqueurs in the Middle Ages, but the living tradition is a family one, tied to gathering the walnuts around the feast of Saint John on 24 June. The Ordine del Nocino Modenese, an association based in Spilamberto, champions the traditional Modena recipe.
orange-curacao: Curaçao liqueur traces to the laraha, a bitter orange descended from citrus trees the Spanish brought to the island in the 16th century, whose fruit turned too bitter to eat in the dry climate but whose peel proved fragrant. After the Dutch West India Company took the island, Amsterdam's Bols says its distillers turned the peel into liqueur, and curaçao came to mean an orange liqueur wherever it was made. On the island itself, the Senior family has sold its own since the late 19th century, and it is made today at Landhuis Chobolobo.
peach-schnapps: Peach schnapps is an American creation of the 1980s, when sweet, fruit-flavoured liqueurs sold under the German word schnapps became a bar craze. DeKuyper's Peachtree led the way and was a hit from its first full year on sale in 1985, and drinks such as the Fuzzy Navel, with orange juice, spread with it. The name borrows from German and Austrian Schnaps, but those are unsweetened fruit brandies, while the American version is a sweet liqueur built for mixing.
triple-sec: Triple sec emerged in 19th-century France, and two houses lay claim to it. Combier says Jean-Baptiste Combier and his wife Josephine created it in Saumur in 1834, drying orange peels and distilling them, while Cointreau, launched in Angers in 1875, did most to make triple sec famous and is sometimes credited with coining the term. By the 1878 Paris Exposition Universelle several distillers were showing orange liqueurs under the name. Nobody agrees what the triple meant, whether triple distillation, three kinds of orange or simply a boast.
umeshu: Umeshu grew out of Japan's long use of the ume, a fruit grown there for centuries and valued in traditional medicine, and recipes for steeping it in spirit with sugar appear in Edo-period writings. For most of its history it was a household drink, made each early summer when the green fruit is picked and kept for months or years to mellow. Commercial producers such as Choya brought it to shops in the second half of the 20th century, but making umeshu at home remains a family custom, and many households still keep their own recipe.
clairin: Clairin is Haiti's own cane spirit, descended from the rough rums made on the island's colonial sugar plantations, which were worked by enslaved Africans. It became the village spirit of rural Haiti, distilled at hundreds of small guildives from fresh cane juice or syrup with wild fermentation, and it has a place in Vodou ceremony as well as daily life. It stayed almost unknown abroad until Italian importer Luca Gargano of La Maison & Velier began bottling clairins from individual producers this century, and Haiti now certifies them under its HaïRum mark.
dark-rum: Dark rum is a style rather than a place, the heavy, molasses-rich rum associated with the British Caribbean, Bermuda and the Royal Navy, whose daily ration was built on dark blends from Jamaica and Guyana. Its colour comes from long ageing, caramel or both, and it has no single inventor. Bermuda's Goslings is a classic example: James Gosling set up shop on the island in the early 19th century, and the family's rum was named Black Seal after the black wax that sealed its bottles. Goslings holds the trademark on the Dark 'n' Stormy, so an official one is made with its rum.
demerara-rum: Demerara rum takes its name from the Demerara River and the old colony around it in what is now Guyana, where sugar estates, worked first by enslaved Africans and later by indentured labourers, each ran their own stills. The colony had around 180 estate distilleries in the mid-19th century, but consolidation left only Diamond, run by Demerara Distillers, which gathered the historic wooden stills of the closed estates. Among them are the Port Mourant double wooden pot still, which the company dates to the 18th century, and the Enmore still, the last wooden Coffey still in the world.
gold-rum: Gold rum has no single birthplace or inventor: it is a style label used across the Caribbean for rums that sit between white and dark, usually coloured by time in oak and often adjusted with caramel.
jamaican-rum: Jamaican rum grew on the island's sugar estates after England seized Jamaica from Spain in the mid-17th century, and its heavy, high-ester style was built on molasses, dunder and slow wild fermentation on plantations worked by enslaved Africans. The word hogo, from the French haut goût, came to describe its pungent, fruity funk. Estates such as Appleton, Hampden and Worthy Park have long histories of distilling, and some still keep muck pits, aged reservoirs of fermentation residue, to build esters. Jamaica Rum is now a protected geographical indication on the island.
overproof-rum: Overproof rum takes its name from the old British way of measuring strength. Before hydrometers, spirit was poured on gunpowder and lit: if the powder still burned, the spirit was proved, and the British standard later fixed 100 proof at about 57% ABV. Anything stronger was over proof, a term that stuck to high-strength rums across the Caribbean. Jamaica's white overproof rums, Wray & Nephew the most famous, are part of local life, and other islands and makers bottle their own for punches and flamed tiki garnishes.
rhum-agricole: Rhum agricole grew from a crisis in the French Caribbean, as European beet sugar undercut cane during the 19th century and estates in Martinique began fermenting fresh cane juice instead of making sugar and molasses. Clément's own history credits Homère Clément, who bought the Acajou estate in 1887 and turned it to rhum made from cane juice. The 1902 eruption of Mount Pelée, which destroyed the rum port of Saint-Pierre, reshaped the island's industry, and in 1996 Martinique rhum agricole became the first rum to receive a French AOC.
spiced-rum: Spiced rum as a major category dates to 1984, when Seagram launched Captain Morgan Original Spiced Rum in the United States, building on a brand it had created four decades earlier. The name honours Sir Henry Morgan, the 17th-century Welsh privateer who later became lieutenant governor of Jamaica, although he had nothing to do with making rum. The success of its vanilla-forward recipe brought a wave of spiced rums from other producers, and Diageo has owned the brand since 2001.
white-rum: White rum in its modern, light style is usually credited to Facundo Bacardí Massó, a Catalan-born wine merchant in Santiago de Cuba, who founded his company there on 4 February 1862. He is credited with using charcoal filtration and blending distillates of different character to make a cleaner, lighter rum than the heavy spirits of the day, and his wife, Amalia, suggested the fruit bats in the distillery's rafters as its emblem. Cuban light rum became the base of the daiquiri and mojito, and after the Revolution Bacardí moved abroad, with its distillery at Cataño, Puerto Rico, becoming its largest.
blended-malt-scotch: Blended malt goes back to 1853, when Edinburgh merchant Andrew Usher began selling Old Vatted Glenlivet, a marriage of malts of different ages that is often cited as the first branded vatted whisky. For most of its life the style was known as vatted malt, a mix of single malts from more than one distillery without any grain whisky, until the Scotch Whisky Regulations of 2009 renamed it blended malt. Brands such as Monkey Shoulder and the whiskies of Compass Box have since made the category familiar.
blended-scotch: Blended Scotch was made possible by the Spirits Act of 1860, which allowed malt and grain whiskies to be mixed in bond before duty was paid. Merchants such as Andrew Usher in Edinburgh, and grocers and wine merchants like John Walker in Kilmarnock, the Dewars in Perth and the Chivas brothers in Aberdeen, used the lighter column-still grain whisky to soften heavy malts into a consistent product. When phylloxera devastated the vineyards of Cognac later in the century, blends filled the gap abroad, and they still make up the large majority of Scotch sold.
campbeltown-single-malt: Campbeltown's whisky boom followed the Excise Act of 1823, which made licensed distilling worthwhile, and the small port on the Kintyre peninsula went on to host around 30 distilleries and call itself the whisky capital of the world. Overproduction and a reputation for poor quality, followed by American Prohibition and the Depression, closed almost all of them in the early 20th century. Springbank and Glen Scotia survived, Springbank's owners revived Glengyle in 2004 to make Kilkerran, and Campbeltown remains one of Scotland's protected whisky regions.
highland-single-malt: The Highland region began as a tax line: the Wash Act of 1784 drew a boundary across Scotland and taxed Highland distillers differently from those in the Lowlands, and the divide stuck. North of it lay a huge, scattered territory of small licensed and illicit stills, many of which went legal after the Excise Act of 1823. Today's Highland region, defined in the 2009 Scotch Whisky Regulations, still stretches from near Glasgow to the far north coast and officially takes in every island except Islay, which is why its malts range so widely in style.
island-single-malt: Island whisky is a popular grouping rather than a legal one, since Scotland's regulations count every island distillery except those on Islay as Highland. Its oldest working distilleries both date from 1798, Highland Park on Orkney and Tobermory on Mull, and Talisker on Skye and Jura followed early in the 19th century. Arran's distillery opened at Lochranza in the 1990s after a long gap on the island, and newer arrivals on Raasay, Harris and elsewhere have extended the group, each drawing on its own island's water, peat and weather.
islay-single-malt: Islay's oldest working distillery, Bowmore, was founded in 1779 by local merchant John Simson, and the island's legal whisky industry grew from there alongside a long tradition of illicit stills. Peat, the island's main fuel, was used to dry the barley, giving Islay malts the smoky, maritime character they became famous for in blends and later as single malts. Today around ten distilleries work on an island of only about 3,000 people, among them Laphroaig, Lagavulin and Ardbeg on the south coast and Port Ellen, recently brought back to life.
lowland-single-malt: The Lowland region dates from the Wash Act of 1784, which divided Scotland along a Highland line and taxed the southern distillers, many of them large commercial operations, more heavily. Lowland malts became known for a light, gentle style, helped by triple distillation at some distilleries, which earned them the nickname Lowland Ladies. Closures in the late 20th century left only a handful, with Auchentoshan near Glasgow keeping triple distillation alive, but new distilleries such as Kingsbarns, Lindores Abbey and Clydeside and the revived Rosebank have rebuilt the region.
single-grain-scotch: Grain whisky began with the continuous still: Robert Stein's design was put to work in the 1820s, including at the Haig family's Cameronbridge distillery in Fife, and Aeneas Coffey's improved version, patented in 1830, became the industry standard. Column stills could turn wheat, maize and barley into light spirit quickly and cheaply, and once blending was allowed, grain whisky became the quiet backbone of nearly every blended Scotch. Distilleries such as Cameronbridge, Girvan and North British have since had single grains bottled on their own, the single meaning one distillery rather than one cereal.
speyside-single-malt: Speyside's legal whisky history is usually dated to 1824, when George Smith of Glenlivet, who is often said to have been the first distiller in Scotland to take out a licence under the new Excise Act, went legal after years in which the glens around the River Spey were known for illicit whisky. Others followed, and the arrival of the railway later in the century made the valley a supplier to the blending houses, which bought much of its fruity malt. Speyside now packs around 50 distilleries, Macallan, Glenfiddich and Glenlivet among them, into a small area and is recognised as its own protected region.
grain-vodka: Vodka's birthplace is disputed between Poland and Russia, and both trace grain spirits to the late Middle Ages: the Polish word wódka appears in court records from Sandomierz in 1405, though it then meant medicines and cosmetics, while Russian accounts credit monks of the Moscow Kremlin, a claim popularised by the Soviet historian William Pokhlebkin. Grain, mostly rye and wheat, became the classic base across the vodka belt, and column stills later made the clean, neutral style possible. US rules long defined vodka as having no distinctive character, wording the regulators eventually dropped.
potato-vodka: Potato vodka arrived after the potato itself, which reached Europe from the Andes in the 16th century and became a widespread crop in Central and Eastern Europe during the 18th and 19th centuries. Cheap and plentiful, potatoes became a common base for spirits in Poland, Germany and the Baltic region, especially once industrial distilling made their starch easier to convert. Grain later regained the larger share, so potato vodka became a speciality, with Polish producers such as Luksusowa and Chopin keeping the style prominent.
aquavit: Aquavit takes its name from the Latin aqua vitae, water of life, and its first known Scandinavian mention comes in a letter of 13 April 1531, in which Eske Bille, lord of Bergenhus castle in Bergen, sent some as a medicine to Olav Engelbrektsson, the last Catholic archbishop of Norway. Grain and later potato spirit flavoured with caraway or dill became the national styles of Denmark, Sweden and Norway. Norway's Linie aquavit keeps an old custom of sending casks by ship across the equator and back before bottling, a voyage its makers credit with mellowing the spirit.
awamori: Awamori was born of trade: distillation reached the Ryukyu Kingdom from Siam in the 15th century, which is why it is still made from long-grain Thai indica rice with black koji mould. The name awamori first appears in a 17th-century record of a royal gift from the Ryukyu king to the Tokugawa shogun, and the spirit was sent to the shogunate as tribute for generations. Okinawa's prized old kusu, some said to be centuries old, were largely lost in the Battle of Okinawa during the Second World War, and producers have been rebuilding aged stocks ever since.
baijiu: Baijiu has no single birthday: drinks resembling it are described in Tang dynasty poetry, and distilling matured into something close to the modern spirit by the Ming dynasty, when Li Shizhen described it in his Compendium of Materia Medica. Each region developed its own grains, fermentation pits and qu cultures, and in the 20th century tasters sorted them into aroma styles such as strong, light, sauce and rice. Kweichow Moutai from Guizhou drew international attention with a medal at the Panama-Pacific Exposition in San Francisco, and baijiu remains overwhelmingly a drink of China.
feni: Feni is Goa's own spirit, and coconut feni, distilled from fermented palm sap, is generally thought to be the older of its two kinds. Cashew feni came after the Portuguese brought the cashew tree to Goa from Brazil during the colonial era, and villagers began fermenting the juicy cashew apples left after the nuts were taken. It is still distilled twice in small country stills, often in clay or copper pots, and cashew feni was the first Indian spirit to receive a geographical indication, with Goa later naming feni a heritage spirit in law.
shochu: Shochu's oldest written record is a piece of graffiti dated 1559, left on a beam of the Kōriyama Hachiman shrine in Isa, Kagoshima, by two carpenters complaining that the stingy head priest never once offered them shochu. Distillation had probably reached southern Kyushu through trade with the rest of Asia, and the region developed its sweet potato shochu after the crop arrived from the Ryukyus in the Edo period. Column stills arrived in the Meiji era, creating a second, lighter style, and by 2003 shochu shipments in Japan had overtaken those of sake.
soju: Soju dates to the Goryeo era, when Mongol armies brought the technique of distilling to Korea in the 13th century, and places where they were based, such as Andong and Kaesong, became known for rice soju. For centuries it was a distilled rice spirit, until the government banned making spirits from rice during postwar food shortages and producers turned to diluted spirit made from sweet potatoes and tapioca. That lighter style, sold by brands such as Jinro, became Korea's everyday drink, while traditional distilled soju has made a comeback since the ban was lifted.
canadian-whisky: Canadian whisky grew out of the flour mills of Upper Canada, where millers turned surplus grain into spirit. Toronto's Gooderham and Worts began making whisky in 1837, Hiram Walker opened his flour mill and distillery across the river from Detroit in 1858, and J.P. Wiser and Joseph Seagram were close behind. Adding a little rye to wheat and corn whisky for flavour gave Canadian whisky its nickname of rye, which the law still accepts. Exports during American Prohibition enriched the big distillers, and Canadian rules still allow a small share of other spirits or wine in the blend.
indian-single-malt: India has made whisky since the colonial era, but most of it was blended from molasses spirit; single malt arrived in 2004, when Bangalore's Amrut Distilleries, founded in 1948 by J.N. Radhakrishna Rao Jagdale, launched its single malt in Scotland to test it against Scotch on home ground. Amrut Fusion drew international praise, and Goa's Paul John and Rampur in Uttar Pradesh followed with single malts of their own. The tropical heat ages spirit fast, and Indian distillers lose far more to evaporation each year than Scottish ones.
japanese-whisky: Japanese whisky began with Shinjiro Torii of Kotobukiya, the company that became Suntory, who built Japan's first malt whisky distillery at Yamazaki, near Kyoto, in 1923. He hired Masataka Taketsuru, who had studied chemistry in Glasgow and apprenticed at the Longmorn and Hazelburn distilleries in 1919 and 1920, and their first whisky, Shirofuda, appeared in 1929. Taketsuru left in 1934 to found the company that became Nikka, at Yoichi in Hokkaido, and the two houses shaped the style. Industry standards adopted in 2021 now define what may be called Japanese whisky.
taiwanese-single-malt: Taiwanese single malt is a 21st-century story. After the island ended its state alcohol monopoly, the King Car Group built the Kavalan distillery in Yuanshan, Yilan county, and first distilled spirit there on 11 March 2006. Its first whisky appeared in 2008, and in 2015 Kavalan Solist Vinho Barrique was named World's Best Single Malt at the World Whiskies Awards, a result that drew attention to subtropical maturation. The state-owned Taiwan Tobacco and Liquor Corporation's Nantou distillery has since released single malts of its own.
scottish-gin: Scotland's gin story rests on its whisky industry, whose grain distilleries, stills and know-how gave it the capacity to make gin on a large scale. Diageo's Cameronbridge distillery in Fife produces Gordon's and Tanqueray, and William Grant & Sons launched Hendrick's from its Girvan grain distillery at the end of the last century, helping start the modern gin boom. A wave of craft gins followed, among them The Botanist from Bruichladdich on Islay, many using native botanicals, and Scotland now distils around 70% of the gin made in the UK.
plymouth-gin: Plymouth Gin has been made since 1793 at the Black Friars Distillery in Plymouth's Barbican, in a building whose oldest parts date from the 15th century and which local tradition links to a Dominican friary and to the Pilgrim Fathers, said to have stayed there before sailing on the Mayflower. Coates & Co. ran it for most of its history, and the Royal Navy's taste for its softer, earthier gin carried it around the world. Plymouth was long one of the few gins with protected status, but its owners chose not to renew that protection, which lapsed in 2015.
english-whisky: England made whisky in the 19th century, but the last distilleries of that era had closed or moved away by the early twentieth century, and the modern revival came about a hundred years later. St George's Distillery in Norfolk, run by the English Whisky Co., was among the first of the new wave, and others followed from the Cotswolds and the Lake District to Cornwall, free to experiment with grains, casks and peat with no inherited house style. After an application backed by the English Whisky Guild, English whisky has since won protected geographical indication status in the UK.
pimms-no-1: Pimm's begins with James Pimm, a Kent farmer's son who opened an oyster bar in the City of London in 1823 and served a gin-based house cup flavoured with liqueurs and fruit extracts. He poured it into a small tankard known as a No. 1 cup, which gave the drink its name, and its popularity led him to produce it on a larger scale for other bars by the mid-19th century. Later numbers used other spirits, such as Scotch for No. 2 and brandy for No. 3, but the gin-based No. 1 became the one tied to English summer garden parties and Wimbledon.
welsh-whisky: Welsh whisky in its modern form dates from 2000, when the Penderyn distillery in the Brecon Beacons began production; its first bottles went on sale on St David's Day in 2004. Wales had an earlier attempt: the Welsh Whisky Distillery at Frongoch, near Bala, opened in the late 19th century but was wound up early in the 20th, and its buildings later became an internment camp for Irish prisoners after the Easter Rising. Penderyn's still was designed by Dr David Faraday, and other Welsh distilleries have since joined it in making whisky.
eau-de-vie: Eau-de-vie is French for water of life, the same idea as the Latin aqua vitae, and in this sense it means a clear spirit distilled from fermented fruit and bottled unaged. The style has no single inventor; it grew from the orchard distilling of Alsace, the Black Forest, Switzerland and neighbouring regions, where farms turned surplus cherries, plums, pears and berries into spirit. Alsace in particular built a reputation for it, with family distilleries in places such as the Val de Villé making kirsch, mirabelle, framboise and poire, berries often being macerated in spirit before distilling.
marc: Marc is the French name for the solid remains of winemaking, the grape skins, seeds and stalks, and for the brandy distilled from them. Like Italy's grappa, it began as a way for wine growers to make use of what the press left behind, and each wine region developed its own, with Burgundy, Champagne and Alsace producing the most famous. Several now carry protected names, such as Marc de Bourgogne, Marc de Champagne and Marc d'Alsace Gewurztraminer, the last distilled from the pomace of a single aromatic grape variety.
grand-marnier: Grand Marnier was created in 1880 by Louis-Alexandre Marnier, who had married Julia Lapostolle, granddaughter of Jean-Baptiste Lapostolle, whose family distillery at Neauphle-le-Château dated from 1827. Marnier blended cognac with the distilled essence of bitter Caribbean oranges. The name is said to have been suggested by his friend César Ritz, the hotelier, as a playful contrast to the fashion for calling things petit, and the liqueur was soon poured at the Ritz and the Savoy. Campari bought the company in 2016.
suze: Suze was brought to market at the 1889 Exposition Universelle in Paris by the Moureaux family's distillery at Maisons-Alfort, near the capital. Two stories explain the name, neither confirmed: one says it honours a sister-in-law named Suzanne, the other the Suze river in Switzerland, where the recipe is said to have been acquired. Its sharp gentian bitterness made it a café classic in France, and its bottle entered art history when Picasso included it in his 1912 collage Glass and Bottle of Suze, now at the Kemper Art Museum in St. Louis.
izarra: Izarra, Basque for star, was created in 1906 in Hendaye, in the French Basque Country, by Joseph Grattau, a botanist and pharmacist, and production moved to Bayonne a few years later. Like Chartreuse it is made in a green and a yellow version, built from a distillate of plants and spices with macerations of prunes and walnut husks, then blended with armagnac. The Grattau family owned it until Cointreau bought it in 1981, and after later changes of ownership it is now distributed by the Vedrenne group.
pineau-des-charentes: Pineau des Charentes is the traditional aperitif of the cognac country, made by adding young cognac to fresh grape must, which halts fermentation and holds on to the fruit's sugar. Charentais tradition traces it to a lucky accident during a late sixteenth-century harvest, when must is said to have been poured into a cask that still held brandy, a legend rather than a record. For centuries it was mostly a family drink, kept for weddings and celebrations, until growers began selling it more widely in the nineteen-twenties, and it gained its own AOC at the end of the Second World War.
floc-de-gascogne: Floc de Gascogne is Gascony's fortified grape must, an old farm recipe of roughly two parts fresh grape juice to one part young armagnac, long made by Gascon families for their own tables before it was sold under a shared name. That name, which appeared in the mid-twentieth century, comes from the Gascon flòc, a bouquet of flowers. Floc later gained its own AOC, and its rules require the must and the armagnac to come from the same estate.
korenwijn: Korenwijn, grain wine, is the style closest to old Dutch and Belgian jenever, made with a high share of malt wine, the pot-distilled spirit of rye, wheat and malted barley that gave early jenever its body. When lighter jonge jenever arrived in the 20th century, made mostly from neutral spirit, the older, maltier style kept its own name and rules. It is often rested in oak and traditionally served in a brimful tulip glass, the first sip taken by bending down to the glass rather than lifting it, part of the Dutch ritual known as the kopstootje.
beerenburg: Beerenburg takes its name from Hendrik Beerenburg, a spice merchant who opened a shop on the Stromarkt in Amsterdam in 1724 and sold a mixture of herbs and roots for customers to steep in their own jenever. He kept his recipe secret, but the idea travelled north, and Friesland adopted it so thoroughly that the drink became a Frisian institution, with local houses such as Sonnema in Dokkum and Weduwe Joustra in Sneek bottling their own blends. Each house guards a different mix of gentian, bay, juniper and other herbs.
elixir-danvers: Elixir d'Anvers was created in 1863 by François-Xavier de Beukelaer, who worked out the recipe after years of experiment and first made it at a distillery on Antwerp's Paardenmarkt. In 1894 the company moved to the Haantjeslei, where the liqueur is still made. Its 32 plants and herbs are macerated, distilled and aged in oak over about five months, and his son Emile de Beukelaer, a racing cyclist in his youth, later became the first president of the UCI, cycling's world governing body.
mandarine-napoleon: Mandarine Napoléon was commercialised in 1892 by Louis Schmidt, a Belgian chemist with a small distillery in Brussels, who said he had rediscovered a recipe linked to Antoine-François de Fourcroy, chemist to Napoleon. The Schmidt distillery closed after the Second World War, and ownership passed to a firm that happened to share the chemist's name, Fourcroy. The Dutch liqueur house De Kuyper bought the brand in 2009, and the liqueur is still made in Belgium.
korn: Korn is one of Germany's oldest spirits: a 1507 decision of the council of Nordhausen, in Thuringia, taxing grain spirit is often cited as its first record, and the town became the most famous Korn centre, with Westphalia and Emsland building strong traditions too. In 1789 Nordhausen set a purity rule requiring its Korn to be made from at least two thirds rye, with barley for the rest. Modern law reserves the name for spirit distilled only from cereal grains, with a stronger grade, Kornbrand or Doppelkorn, above it, and Korn remains a fixture of northern Germany.
obstler: Obstler belongs to the farm distilling tradition of southern Germany, Austria and South Tyrol, where orchard owners have long turned windfall and surplus apples and pears into spirit. It has no single inventor or founding date; its home is the small farm still, and in Germany thousands of farms have held rights to distil a fixed quantity of their own fruit each year. It is distilled from fermented whole fruit, and alongside the classic apple and pear blend, many makers now bottle single-variety versions from particular orchards.
steinhager: Steinhäger is the juniper spirit of Steinhagen, in Westphalia near Bielefeld, a town with a long tradition of juniper distilling. The H. W. Schlichte house, which dates its production to 1766, is among the oldest that survive, and the town's distillers made their name by fermenting and distilling the juniper berries themselves before blending the result with grain spirit. Sold in grey-brown stoneware crocks, Steinhäger became one of Germany's familiar schnapps, and its name is legally protected for spirits made in Steinhagen.
jagermeister: Jägermeister was launched in 1935 by Curt Mast, son of a vinegar maker and wine trader in Wolfenbüttel, Lower Saxony, who had developed the herbal liqueur the year before. Its name, master of the hunt, was the title used for senior foresters and gamekeepers, and it had gained new prominence through the national hunting law passed in 1934. The stag with a glowing cross on the label recalls the legend of Saint Hubertus, patron saint of hunters. American importer Sidney Frank built its fame abroad in the 1980s, and the company is still based in Wolfenbüttel.
weinbrand: Weinbrand's story begins in 1892, when Hugo Asbach founded his distillery in Rüdesheim am Rhein and sold his brandy as Rüdesheim cognac. A 1907 Asbach label already used the word Weinbrand, and after the Treaty of Versailles reserved cognac for French brandy, the term became the official German name, fixed in wine law in 1923. Asbach Uralt became the defining brand, and from 1924 the company also sold chocolates filled with brandy, which remain a Christmas staple in Germany.
danziger-goldwasser: Danziger Goldwasser traces to Ambrosius Vermöllen, a Dutchman from the village of De Lier who became a citizen of Danzig in 1598 and founded a liqueur business there. In 1704 his descendants moved to new premises in the Breitgasse whose façade bore a salmon, which gave the house its name, Der Lachs. Gold leaf was prized as medicine at the time, and its flakes became the drink's signature. After 1945, when the city became Gdańsk in Poland, only the company's Berlin branch carried on, and since 1971 Der Lachs has been made in Nörten-Hardenberg in Germany.
eierlikor: German egg liqueur took its commercial form in 1876, when the Antwerp distiller Eugen Verpoorten opened a liqueur and colonial goods business in Heinsberg, in the Rhineland, and began producing it to a recipe the company says has not changed since. The firm later moved to Berlin and, after the Second World War, to Bonn, where it is still family-run, and its slogan Ei, ei, ei, Verpoorten made it a household name. Eierlikör is a fixture of German baking and Christmas markets, where it is often served in small edible waffle cups.
underberg: Underberg was founded on 17 June 1846, the day of Hubert Underberg's wedding in Rheinberg on the Lower Rhine, when he set up the company H. Underberg-Albrecht to make a herbal bitter. The recipe has stayed within the family ever since, and its herbs are macerated and rested in oak before bottling. In 1949 his grandson Emil Underberg introduced the 20 ml single-portion bottle wrapped in straw-coloured paper, which became the form most people know it by.
marillenbrand: Marillenbrand is Austria's apricot brandy, and its heartland is the Wachau, the stretch of the Danube valley between Melk and Krems where apricot orchards grow alongside the vineyards. Distilling apricots there grew out of the local farm and winery tradition rather than any single founder, and the fruit itself became a regional emblem. Wachauer Marille is now a protected designation of origin for apricots grown in the Wachau and neighbouring communities, and Wachauer Marillenbrand is protected as a spirit too; the trees flower early, so a spring frost can cost much of a year's crop.
stroh: Stroh traces to 1832, when Sebastian Stroh began making liqueurs and spirits commercially in Klagenfurt, in Carinthia, where the company is still based. The Habsburg lands had no tropical colonies, so local makers imitated the flavour of cane rum by adding flavourings and colouring to other spirit, a style known as Inländer-Rum, or domestic rum, and Stroh became its leading brand. It won a grand gold medal at the 1900 Paris Exposition Universelle, and Austrians use it in baking, in Jagertee and in hot punches.
zirbenschnaps: Zirbenschnaps is a herbal liqueur of the Tyrolean Alps, made by steeping the young cones of the Swiss stone pine in spirit, and it comes from a mountain household tradition with no recorded inventor or founding date.
enzian: Enzian is the gentian brandy of the Alps, distilled from the roots of the yellow gentian dug on mountain slopes. In Bavaria its best-documented home is Berchtesgaden, where the Grassl distillery, regarded as Germany's oldest gentian distillery, traces its history to 1602 and still digs roots in the surrounding mountains. Parts of the Alps were already restricting root digging by the late 17th century, and because the plant grows slowly, wild harvesting remains tightly regulated across most of the range.
damassine: Damassine is distilled only from the small red damassine plum of the Swiss canton of Jura, especially the Ajoie, where the fruit has been grown for generations. Its origins are wrapped in legend: the name points to Damascus, and the usual story says crusaders brought the plum's stone back from the Holy Land in the twelfth century. What is documented is its modern protection as a Swiss AOP, which sets the growing area and methods for the eau-de-vie.
appenzeller-alpenbitter: Appenzeller Alpenbitter was first produced in 1902 by Emil Ebneter in Appenzell, who experimented with home distillates of his region's medicinal herbs until he arrived at the bitter's recipe. In 1908 he founded Emil Ebneter & Co. with his brother-in-law, Beat Kölbener, and the business has stayed with the founding families ever since, renamed Appenzeller Alpenbitter AG in 2006. The recipe has been changed only once, in 1960, and remains a closely kept secret.
